newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's De Klerk seeks to protect his name.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's De Klerk seeks to protect his name.

text.p: Former president F.W. de Klerk, battling to defend his reputation against allegations of human rights violations, on Thursday said he would appeal to South Africa's Human Rights Commission for protection.
De Klerk said in a statement he would ask the commission to set "essential criteria for public remarks by public figures".

He said his decision followed an investigation by his white-led National Party into remarks by deputy minister Peter Mokaba, who recently publicly labelled him "a bald-headed criminal dripping with the blood of innocent people."

The ruling African National Congress (ANC) is also pointing a finger at De Klerk and his party. It said in a statement on Thursday De Klerk's party was to blame for the "cold-blooded murders" and "secret burials" of ANC cadres, some of whose bodies were exhumed from secret graves.

"The moral and political responsibility... lies squarely on the shoulders of the National Party regime," the ANC said. "No amount of denials by respective leaders of the NP including F.W. de Klerk can convince the public and the international community that apartheid was no crime against humanity in the face of these exhumations."

The NP said it also investigated remarks by Deputy Defence Minister Ronnie Kasrils and Transport Minister Mac Maharaj, who have accused de Klerk of condoning the assassination of anti-apartheid activists during the final decade of white rule.
Evidence to Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission on human rights under apartheid has increasingly pointed to cabinet knowledge of police hit squads.
De Klerk has insisted he was unaware of the activities of police and military units that tortured and killed activists and that there was no "third force" during his years as president.

"It is a lie that I knew. It's a lie that I was part of any conspiracy to do these terrible things... to assassinate people," he said after new evidence two weeks ago appeared to link him to a cabinet discussion about state hit squads.

On Wednesday, government-appointed independent investigator Howard Varney said he had given a 150-page file to the truth commission and to the minister in charge of the police. He said it showed de Klerk attended a State Security Council meeting about plans for a third force to "wipe out terrorists."
The council was an inner cabinet that managed the war against Nelson Mandela's ANC and groups hostile to white rule.
De Klerk, who repudiated apartheid in 1990 and later set the stage for democracy, said he would consider legal action if the Human Rights Commission did not adequately protect him.
